# Time-Optimal APSP and Matrix Multiplication in Classes of Linear Neighborhood Complexity

**Abstract**

The notion of _linear neighborhood complexity_ is a very general structural assumption on a graph class, covering most classes of sparse graphs such as planar graphs, graphs excluding a fixed (topological) minor, or bounded expansion graphs, as well as many structured classes of dense graphs, such as graphs of bounded clique-width, twin-width, merge-width, or flip-width.

In this work, we present O(_n_<sup>2</sup>)-time optimal algorithms for _n_-vertex graphs coming from a class of linear neighborhood complexity for the following problems:

\(\bullet\) All-Pairs Shortest Paths,

\(\bullet\) the multiplication of the adjacency matrix _M_ of the input graph with any \(n\times n\) matrix. More specifically, after a quadratic preprocessing, we can multiply _M_ with any _n_-vector in O(_n_) time.

This solves several questions raised in [Bonnet, Kim, Geniet, Moon; ICALP ’26], and improves and generalizes results in several other recent papers [Bonnet, Giocanti, Ossona de Mendez, Thomassé; STACS ’23], [Bannach, Marwitz, Tantau; STACS ’24], [Anand, van den Brand, McCarty; NeurIPS ’26], [Kozma, Oppler ’26], and [Cardinal, McCarty, Yuditsky ’26]. We also extend our results to classes of bounded VC density.

In classes of linear neighborhood complexity, we also give a triangle-detection algorithm in randomized linear time O(_n+m_) in _n_-vertex _m_-edge graphs, a _K_<sub>4</sub>-detection algorithm in randomized O(_n_log<sup>5</sup>_n+m_log_n_) or deterministic O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time, and a _K_<sub>5</sub>-detection algorithm in randomized O(_n_log<sup>9</sup>_n+m_log<sup>5</sup>_n_) time.

## 1 Introduction

In recent years, we have witnessed tremendous progress in understanding very general structured graph classes and their algorithmic properties.

Classic studies of structured graph classes tackle topologically constrained graphs such as planar graphs, or, more generally, graph classes excluding a minor \[40\]. This is probably the limit of improved tractability for some algorithmic problems, e.g., network design problems, where topological restrictions on the input graph seem necessary. However, for problems that treat unweighted graphs and interactions between vertices only within a bounded distance, we expect to find efficient algorithms in more general graph classes. Problems of this type include NP-hard problems such as Minimum Dominating Set or Maximum Independent Set (where one can hope for approximation or parameterized algorithms that are believed to be impossible for general graphs) and polynomial-time solvable problems such as multiple shortest path computations (where one can hope to beat known lower bounds that hold in general graphs).

Two decades ago, Nešetřil and Ossona de Mendez \[43, 44, 45, 46\] initiated the study of _bounded expansion_ and _nowhere dense_ graph classes. Subsequent research confirmed that the latter are the limit of tractability of first-order model checking (a meta-problem capturing most problems that concern bounded-distance interactions between vertices) among subgraph-closed graph classes \[30\]. However, the assumption of being subgraph-closed does not allow this theory to capture _dense_ structured graph classes. In attempts to understand the limit of tractability of first-order model checking on graphs in full generality, width parameters twin-width \[16\], flip-width \[48\], and merge- width \[24\] were introduced. Boundedness of the last two is conjectured to be equivalent; furthermore, tractability of the first-order model checking problem in hereditary graph classes is conjectured to be delimited by the slightly more general notions of _almost bounded flip-width_ or _almost bounded merge-width_ \[24\]. Research on algorithms for classes of bounded twin-width/merge-width/flip-width includes not only parameterized algorithms for first-order model checking \[16, 28, 24\], but also parameterized algorithms for specific problems \[13, 14, 29, 4\], approximation algorithms \[13, 7, 22\], polynomial kernels \[15\], and polynomial-time algorithms \[13, 37, 31, 12, 23\].

However, most of the above-mentioned algorithms require a witness of low twin-width or merge- width to be given as part of the input. The existence of polynomial-time or parameterized algorithms providing appropriate witnesses remains a central open question in the area.

First-order formulas are able to speak about any fixed distance between vertices, but some problems are concerned only with direct adjacencies. This makes them potentially efficiently solvable on even larger classes of graphs. A promising concept in this direction is the notion of _linear neighborhood complexity_ \[27\]. We say that a graph class C has _linear neighborhood complexity_ if there exists a constant _c\>_0 such that for every \(G\in\mathcal{C}\) and \(\emptyset\neq A\subseteq V(G)\) the number of neighborhood traces on _A_, i.e., \(|\{N(v)\cap A|v\in V(G)\}|\), is at most _c|A_|. We also say that C has VC density \(\rho\) if there exists a constant _c\>_0 such that for every \(G\in\mathcal{C}\) and \(\emptyset\neq A\subseteq V(G)\), \(|\{N(v)\cap A|v\in V(G)\}|\le c|A|^\rho\).

Linear neighborhood complexity not only covers all classes of bounded twin-width, flip-width, and merge-width but also, for example, classes with bounded _weak_ 2_-coloring number_, such as the class of 2-subdivisions of all graphs. An even more general notion--extending graph _degeneracy_ to the dense setting--is bounded _symmetric-difference degeneracy (sd-degeneracy)_ \[11\]. For a graph _G_, it is the least number _c_ such that _G_ can be reduced into a single vertex by iteratively finding two distinct vertices _u,v_ with \(|N(v)\triangle N(u)|\le c\) and removing one of them from the graph. (This notion of a decomposition is called an _sd-degeneracy sequence_. See Section 2 for precise definitions.) We refer to Fig. 1 for an overview of the properties of graph classes mentioned here.

The first algorithmic applications of the linear neighborhood complexity assumption stem from<tbc>

the seminal work of Welzl [49], which implies that for a given _n_-vertex graph from such a class, one can order its vertices in polynomial time so that every neighborhood is a union of O(log_n_) many intervals. The runtime was improved to O((_m+n_)log_n_) in very recent work with O(log<sup>2</sup>_n_) intervals for each vertex [23] instead of O(log_n_). Prior works [19, 25] achieve O(log<sup>2</sup>_n_) intervals on average per vertex in the same running time. In turn, such a representation can be transformed into an sd-degeneracy sequence of width O(log<sup>2</sup>_n_) [12].

Furthermore, [11] introduced a representation of the edge set of the graph, called a _signed tree model_. A signed tree model of a graph _G_ is a binary tree with leaves labeled with _V(G_) and additional transversal edges which can be positive or negative, and which fully determine the adjacency in _G_ (see Section 2 for a precise definition). Subsequent work [12] transformed signed tree models into _interval biclique partitions_, first defined in [13]. An interval biclique partition into _b_ bicliques of a graph _G_ is a labeling of _V(G_) with {1,2_,...,n_} together with a partition of _E(G_) into _b_ bicliques whose sides are intervals of {1,2_,...,n_}. By pipelining the results of [12, 11], we can first turn an sd-degeneracy sequence of width _d_ into a signed tree model with O(_dn_) transversal pairs in O(_dn+m_) time, and then into an interval biclique partition with O(_dn_) bicliques in O(_dn_log_n+m_) time.

While sd-degeneracy sequences, sparse signed tree models, and interval biclique partitions are relatively simple and often efficiently computable, they bypass the need for involved decomposition notions in classes of bounded twin-width/merge-width/flip-width, when the problem at hand lends itself to their algorithmic uses.

## 1.1 Our results

Our first contributions are two time-optimal algorithms for computing sd-degeneracy sequences of bounded width in classes of linear neighborhood complexity.

**Theorem 1.** _For every graph class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity, there is an_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>)_-time algorithm that, given an n-vertex graph_ \(G\in\mathcal{C}\)_, outputs an sd-degeneracy sequence of G of width_ O<sub>C</sub>(1).

Note that the running time of Theorem 1 is optimal for graphs with \(\Theta(n^2)\) edges. This resolves an open problem of \[12\]. For graphs with a subquadratic number of edges, we provide a linear-time randomized algorithm.

**Theorem 2.** _For every graph class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity, there is a randomized algorithm that, given a graph_ \(G\in\mathcal{C}\)_, outputs an sd-degeneracy sequence of G of width_ O<sub>C</sub>(1) _in expected time_ \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}\big(|V(G)|+|E(G)|\big)\).

Previously available algorithms would either proceed by naively constructing an sd-degeneracy sequence of width O(1), which takes time O(_n_<sup>4</sup>) using a direct implementation (or O(_n_<sup>3</sup>) after realizing that C has bounded versatile symmetric difference, see definition below), or by following Welzl’s approach, which currently yields an sd-degeneracy sequence of width O(log<sup>2</sup>_n_) in time O((_n+m_)log_n_) \[23, 12\], where _n_=|_V(G_)| and _m_=|_E(G_)|.

To prove Theorem 1, we introduce the notion of _bounded versatile symmetric difference_, where we require that every induced subgraph with _n_ vertices contains \(\Theta(n)\) disjoint vertex pairs _u,v_ satisfying \(|N(u)\triangle N(v)|\le c\) for some constant _c_.

On one hand, a simple application of Haussler’s packing lemma (cf. Theorem 33) proves that linear neighborhood complexity implies bounded versatile symmetric difference. On the other hand, we show how to use the "versatility" strengthening, together with a known data structure for longest common extension of \[39\], to compute sd-degeneracy sequences in O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time.

We will actually prove generalizations of Theorems 1 and 2 to classes of VC density \(\rho\).

**Theorem 3.** _For every real number_ \(\rho\ge 1\) _and every graph class_ C _of VC density_ \(\rho\)_, there is an_ \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(n^{3-\frac{1}{\rho}})\)_-time algorithm that, given an n-vertex graph_ \(G\in\mathcal{C}\)_, outputs an sd-degeneracy sequence of G of width_ \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(n^{1-\frac{1}{\rho}})\).

**Theorem 4.** _For every real number_ \(\rho\ge 1\) _and every graph class_ C _of VC density_ \(\rho\)_, there is a randomized algorithm that, given a graph_ \(G\in\mathcal{C}\)_, outputs an sd-degeneracy sequence of G of width_ \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(n^{1-\frac{1}{\rho}})\) _in expected time_ \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}\big(|V(G)|+|E(G)|\big)\).

With the aforementioned results of \[12, 11\], Theorem 1 allows us to compute in O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time a signed tree model with O(_n_) transversal pairs and an interval biclique partition with O(_n_) bicliques. Our second contribution is an efficient algorithm using the latter for shortest-path computation.

**Theorem 5.** _There is an_ O(_n+b)-time algorithm that, given an interval biclique partition of an n-vertex graph G with b bicliques and_ \(s\in V(G)\)_, outputs a shortest-path tree from vertex s in G._

Note that the running time of Theorem 5 is independent of _m_, the number of edges of _G_, and in fact is usually sublinear in _m_. Theorem 5 bypasses the use of the DAG-compression technique \[5\], which is a way to solve shortest-path problems from interval biclique partitions that incurs, in the current state of knowledge, extra superconstant factors.

By applying Theorem 5 to every vertex of the graph and pipelining it with Theorem 1 and the aforementioned results of \[12, 11\], we obtain a time-optimal algorithm for All-Pairs Shortest Path (APSP for short) in classes of linear neighborhood complexity.

**Theorem 6.** _For every graph class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity, All-Pairs Shortest Path can be solved in_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>) _time on n-vertex graphs of_ C.

Previous work on APSP includes an O(_n_<sup>2</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_n_)-time algorithm in classes of bounded twin- width, and in time O(_n_<sup>2</sup>log_n_) on graphs of bounded radius-1 merge-width given with a witness \[12\]. More recently, the O(_n_<sup>2</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_n_)-time APSP algorithm was extended to classes of linear neighborhood complexity \[18\]. In \[13\], an O(_n_<sup>2</sup>log_n_)-time APSP algorithm was given on graphs of bounded twin- width given with their contraction sequence, which was then improved to O(_n_<sup>2</sup>)-time in the paper introducing DAG-compressions \[5\].

Note that Theorems 2 and 5, together with \[12, 11\], also give a randomized O(_kn+m_)-time algorithm for Multi-Source Shortest Path from _k_ sources on _n_-vertex _m_-edge graphs. Another consequence of Theorem 1 and results in \[12\] (see Lemma 14) is:

**Theorem 7.** _For every graph class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity, there is an_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>)_-time algorithm that, given any adjacency matrix M of an n-vertex graph of_ C_, yields a data structure that computes the matrix-vector product MX in time_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_) _for any n-vector X._

_In particular, the product MN can be computed in_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>) _time for any_ \(n\times n\) _matrix N._

We refer to Fig. 2 for a diagram of the algorithmic pipeline discussed in the previous few paragraphs.

Theorem 6 answers \[12, Question 2\] positively, far beyond classes of bounded twin-width (for which the question was asked). Theorems 6 and 7 improve APSP and matrix-multiplication algorithms in \[14, 2, 12, 35, 18\], all of which have extra polylog factors, and extend results in \[36, 5\], which work on graphs of bounded clique-width and on graphs of bounded twin-width given with contraction sequences, respectively.

By using Theorem 3 rather than Theorem 1, one can solve All-Pairs Shortest Path in graphs of VC density \(\rho\) (or multiply the adjacency matrix of graphs of VC density \(\rho\) with any matrix) in time \(\mathcal{O}(n^{3-1/\rho})\). However, we observe that fast matrix multiplication and Seidel’s algorithm \[47\] have a better running time in general instances as soon as \(\rho>1.591\).

We also obtain a time-optimal triangle-detection algorithm in classes of linear neighborhood complexity, which leverages an sd-degeneracy sequence of constant width.

**Theorem 8.** _For every graph class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity, Triangle Detection can be solved in expected time_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n+m_) _on n-vertex m-edge graphs of_ C.

Let us recall that on general graphs, the fastest known Triangle Detection algorithm runs in time \(\mathcal{O}(min(n^\omega,m^{2\omega/(\omega+1)}))\) \[1\] where \(\omega\) is the exponent of square matrix multiplication, which currently implies O(min(_n_<sup>2.372</sup>_,m_<sup>1.407</sup>)) time.

Utilizing both an sd-degeneracy sequence and a Welzl order of the input graph, we obtain randomized almost-linear algorithms for finding 4-vertex and 5-vertex cliques, and a deterministic O(_n_<sup>2</sup>)-time algorithm for _K_<sub>4</sub> detection (time-optimal within dense graphs).

**Theorem 9.** _For every graph class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity, a K_<sub>4</sub> _subgraph can be found in expected_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_log<sup>5</sup>_n+m_log_n_) _or in deterministic_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>) _time on n-vertex m-edge graphs of_ C.

**Theorem 10.** _For every graph class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity, a K_<sub>5</sub> _subgraph can be found in expected time_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_log<sup>9</sup>_n+m_log<sup>5</sup>_n_) _on n-vertex m-edge graphs of_ C.

Prior to our work, no linear-time algorithm was known for Triangle Detection in the much more restricted classes of bounded clique-width, nor was an almost-linear algorithm known in classes of bounded twin-width (where, for both, the input is a mere graph without a witness of low width).

## 2 Preliminaries

We index the word positions from 1. In particular, \(w=w[1]w[2]\cdots w[s]\) for every word _w_ of length _s_. We let log_x_ denote the base-2 logarithm of _x_. For integers \(\ell\unknown r\), let \([\ell,r]\) be the integer interval spanning all values from \(\ell\) to _r_, inclusively, and for integer _n_, let \[_n_\]=\[1_,n_\]. Graphs are simple (without loops or parallel edges), undirected, and finite. For a graph _G_, we denote its vertex- and edge-set as _V(G_) and _E(G_), respectively.

### 2.1 Neighborhood complexity

For a graph _G_, let \(\pi_G(m)\) be the maximum number of distinct neighborhoods of vertices in _G_ restricted to a set of at most _m_ vertices, i.e.,

\(\pi_G(m):=max_{X\subseteq V(G),|X|\unknown m}|\{N_G(v)\cap X:v\in V(G)\}|.\)

We say that _G_ has _c-linear neighborhood complexity_ (or _c_-LNC) if \(\pi_G(m)\unknown c\cdot m\) for all positive \(m\in\mathbb{N}\). Class C has _linear neighborhood complexity_ if there exists a constant _c_ such that all graphs \(G\in\mathcal{C}\) have _c_-LNC. We say that C has _VC density_ \(\rho\) if there exists a constant _c_ such that for all \(G\in\mathcal{C}\), \(\pi_G(m)\unknown cm^\rho\) for all positive _m_. Finally, we say that _G_ has \((c,\rho)\)_-polynomial neighborhood complexity_ (or \((c,\rho)\)-PNC) if \(\pi_G(m)\unknown c\cdot m^\rho\) for all positive \(m\in\mathbb{N}\).

### 2.2 Symmetric difference and sd-degeneracy

In this paper, we define the _symmetric difference_ of two vertices _u,v_ in a graph _G_ as

\(\mathrm{sd}_G(u,v):=|N_G(u)\triangle N_G(v)|,\)

where \(\triangle\) denotes the symmetric difference of two sets: \(X\triangle Y:=(X\backslash Y)\cup(Y\backslash X)\). There are slight variations in defining the symmetric difference of _u,v_ (depending on whether or not _u,v_ themselves count), but they only differ by a constant additive term. We say that two distinct vertices _u,v_ are _d-near-twins_ in _G_ if \(\mathrm{sd}_G(u,v)\unknown d\), and are _twins_ if sd_<sub>G</sub>(u,v_)=0.

The _symmetric difference_ sd(_G_) of a graph _G_ is the least nonnegative integer _d_ such that for every induced subgraph _H_ of _G_ with at least two vertices, there are two _d_-near-twins in _H_.

An _sd-degeneracy sequence_ of an _n_-vertex graph _G_ is a list (_u_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,(u_<sub>_n_-1</sub>_,v_<sub>_n_-1</sub>) of pairs of vertices of _G_ such that

• \(u_i\neq v_i\) for every \(i\in[n-1]\),<tbc>

• _V(G_)={_u_<sub>1</sub>_,u_<sub>2</sub>_,...,u_<sub>_n_-2</sub>_,u_<sub>_n_-1</sub>_,v_<sub>_n_-1</sub>}, and<tbc>

• there is no _i\<j_ such that \(u_i\in\{u_j,v_j\}\).<tbc>

<tbc>Informally, it is an elimination sequence where only the first element of the pair is removed at each step. The _width_ of the sd-degeneracy sequence (_u_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,(u_<sub>_n_-1</sub>_,v_<sub>_n_-1</sub>) is defined as

\(\mathrm{max}_{i\in[n-1]}\mathrm{sd}_{G-\{u_1,u_2,\dots,u_{i-1}\}}(u_i,v_i).\)

The _sd-degeneracy_ of _G_ (where ’sd’ stands for symmetric difference) is the least integer _d_ such that _G_ admits an sd-degeneracy sequence of width _d_.

Equivalently, the class of graphs of sd-degeneracy at most _d_ can be defined by induction on the number of vertices: a graph _G_ has sd-degeneracy at most _d_ if either \(|V(G)|\unknown 1\), or there is a pair of distinct vertices \(u,v\in V(G)\) such that \(\mathrm{sd}_G(u,v)\unknown d\) and the graph _G-u_ has sd-degeneracy at most _d_.

We say that a hereditary graph class C has _bounded versatile symmetric difference_ if there is an integer _d_:=_d_<sub>C</sub>_\>_0 such that for every _n_-vertex graph \(G\in\mathcal{C}\), there are at least \(\lfloor n/d\rfloor\) disjoint pairs of vertices _u,v_ satisfying \(\mathrm{sd}_G(u,v)\le d\). For \(\alpha\in[0,1)\), we say that C has _versatile symmetric difference of exponent_ \(\alpha\) if there is a constant _d_:=_d_<sub>C</sub>_\>_0 such that for every _n_-vertex graph \(G\in\mathcal{C}\), there are \(\lfloor n/d\rfloor\) disjoint pairs of vertices _u,v_ in _G_ satisfying \(\mathrm{sd}_G(u,v)\le dn^\alpha\). Thus _versatile symmetric difference of exponent 0_ coincides with _bounded versatile symmetric difference_.

## 2.3 Signed tree models and interval biclique partitions

We recall the definition of signed tree models for the sake of self-containedness. However, we will not use them in the rest of the paper. Thus, from this subsection, one can only read the definition of interval biclique partitions (given just after Lemma 11) and Lemma 13.

_Signed tree models_, originally defined in \[11\], generalize the tree models introduced in the context of twin-width \[17, 13\]. In a rooted tree _T_ and \(u,v\in V(T)\), by \(u\unknown_Tv\) we denote that _u_ is an ancestor of _v_. A pair of vertices of a rooted tree _T_ is a _transversal pair_ of _T_ if it is not between an ancestor and descendant. We say that two transversal pairs _u_<sub>1</sub>_v_<sub>1</sub> and _u_<sub>2</sub>_v_<sub>2</sub> _cross_ if one of _u_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub> is a strict ancestor of one of _u_<sub>2</sub>_,v_<sub>2</sub>, and conversely, one of _u_<sub>2</sub>_,v_<sub>2</sub> is a strict ancestor of one of _u_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub>.

A _full_ binary tree is a rooted binary tree where every internal node has exactly two children. A _signed tree model_ is a triple T=(_T,A,B_) where _T_ is a full binary tree, _A_ and _B_ are two disjoint sets of transversal pairs of _T_, and \(A\cup B\) does not contain any crossing pair. The transversal pairs of _A_ and _B_ are called _negative edges_ and _positive edges_, respectively.

We say that a transversal pair \(u'v'\) _covers_ the pair \(u,v\in V(T)\) if \(u'\unknown_Tu\) and \(v'\unknown_Tv\) and there is no transversal pair \(u''v''\neq u'v'\) in \(A\cup B\) with \(u'\unknown_Tu''\unknown_Tu\) and \(v'\unknown_Tv''\unknown_Tv\). We denote by _L(T_) the set of leaves of _T_. The graph _G_<sub>T</sub> represented by the signed tree model T has vertex set _L(T_), and \(u,v\in L(T)\) are adjacent in _G_<sub>T</sub> if and only if the pair _u,v_ is covered by a positive transversal pair in T .

A graph class C has _sparse signed tree models_ if there is a constant _c_ such that every \(G\in\mathcal{C}\) admits a signed tree model (_T,A,B_) with \(|A\cup B|\le c\cdot|V(T)|\). There is an efficient algorithm that turns sd-degeneracy sequences of bounded width into sparse signed tree models.

**Lemma 11** (Lemma 18 of \[12\], Lemma 3.1 of \[11\])**.** _There is an_ O(_dn+m)-time algorithm that, given an sd-degeneracy sequence of an n-vertex m-edge graph G of width d, outputs a signed tree model of G with_ O(_dn_) _transversal pairs._

Assume that the graph _G_ comes with a total ordering of its vertices; for convenience, assume that the vertex set of _G_ is \[_n_\], ordered naturally. We then define the _interval biclique partition_ of _G_ as the partitioning of the edge set of _G_ into bicliques, where each side of each biclique is an integer subinterval of \[_n_\]. The following lemma implies that a small-size signed tree model can be efficiently turned into a small-size interval biclique partition.

**Lemma 12** (Item 1 of Theorem 1 of \[12\])**.** _There is an_ O(_p_log_n)-time algorithm that, given a signed tree model of an n-vertex graph G with p transversal pairs, outputs an interval biclique partition of G with_ O(_p_) _bicliques._

We will rely on the following consequence of Lemmas 11 and 12.

**Lemma 13.** _There is an_ O(_dn_log_n+m)-time algorithm that, given an sd-degeneracy sequence of an n-vertex m-edge graph G of width d, outputs an interval biclique partition of G with_ O(_dn_) _bicliques._

### 2.4 Matrix multiplication

An interval biclique partition with O(_n_) bicliques of an _n_-vertex graph _G_ allows one to multiply any adjacency matrix of _G_ with any _n_-vector in O(_n_) time. More precisely:

**Lemma 14** (Theorem 33 in \[12\])**.** _For every abelian group_ A_, there exists an algorithm that takes on input an interval biclique partition with b bicliques of an n-vertex graph G with adjacency matrix M and an n-vector_ \(X\in\mathcal{A}^n\) _and computes the product MX, in time_ O(_n+b_) _and_ O(_n+b_) _group operations._

Note that, as the adjacency matrix _M_ is a {0,1}-matrix, the multiplication of _M_ with a vector of group elements is well-defined. This lemma has a short proof that encodes _M_ into an \(n\times n\left\{-1,0,1\right\}\)- matrix with O(_b_) nonzero entries. As a direct consequence of Lemma 14, one can multiply _M_ with any \(n\times n\) matrix in time O(_n(n+b_)) (assuming the group operations take constant time).

## 3 Finding an sd-degeneracy sequence deterministically

In this section, we provide an algorithm that computes an sd-degeneracy sequence of constant width in graphs of bounded versatile symmetric difference. The algorithm is time-optimal for dense graphs (i.e., _n_-vertex graphs with \(\Theta(n^2)\) edges). More generally, the algorithm computes an sd-degeneracy sequence of width \(\mathcal{O}(n^\alpha)\) in graphs of versatile symmetric difference of exponent \(\alpha\).

It uses classic data structures for strings. Given a word _w_ of finite length _s_, a longest common extension (LCE) query \(i,j\in[s]\) asks for the largest integer _k_ such that \(w[i]w[i+1]\cdots w[i+k-1]=w[j]w[j+1]\cdots w[j+k-1]\).

**Theorem 15** (Section 4 of \[39\])**.** _Fix a finite alphabet_ \(\Sigma\)_. There is an_ O(_s)-time algorithm, that given a word w of length s over_ \(\Sigma\)_, builds a data structure that answers each LCE query on w in constant time._

Theorem 15 is originally shown by reduction to least common ancestor (LCA) in the suffix tree. To avoid computing the suffix tree, one can alternatively go through suffix array, longest common prefix (LCP) array, and range minimum query (RMQ). See \[6\] for a simple proof of optimal LCA and RMQ data structures.

Theorem 15 yields a surprisingly fast check for _d_-near-twinness in graphs.

**Theorem 16.** _There is an_ O(_n_<sup>2</sup>)_-time algorithm that, given an n-vertex graph G, builds a data structure that given a query_ \(u,v\in V(G),d\in\mathbb{N}\) _reports if_ \(sd_G(u,v)\le d\) _in_ O(_d_) _time._

_Proof._ We build a binary word _w_ of length _n_<sup>2</sup> by concatenating the adjacency vectors of all vertices. Formally, assuming _V(G_)=\[_n_\], for every \(a,b\in[n]\), _w_\[(_a_-1)_n+b_\]=1 if \(ab\in E(G)\) and _w_\[(_a_-1)_n+b_\]=0 otherwise. The word _w_ can easily be built in O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time.

By Theorem 15, we build, in O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time, a data structure D_<sub>w</sub>_ that answers each LCE query on _w_ in constant time. Given a query \(u,v\in V(G),d\in\mathbb{N}\), we proceed as follows. We initialize \(p\leftarrow 1\) and \(q\leftarrow d\).

While \(p\le n\) and \(q\ge 0\), we feed D_<sub>w</sub>_ with the query (_u_-1)_n+p,(v_-1)_n+p_. (Note that, for _p_=1, those are the positions where the adjacency vectors of _u_ and _v_, respectively, start.) Let _k_ be the query answer, found in constant time. If \(p+k\le n\), we decrement _q_ by 1 and set \(p\leftarrow p+k+1\), else we exit the while loop.

When we exit the while loop, if \(q\ge 0\), we report that \(sd_G(u,v)\le d\), and otherwise (_q_=-1) that sd_<sub>G</sub>(u,v)\>d_.

**Time.** We have already checked that D_<sub>w</sub>_ is built in O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time. Note that each query _u,v,d_ makes at most _d_+1 LCE queries. Indeed, in the end of the while loop, we decrement _q_ (initially set to _d_) by 1 or we exit the loop, whereas continuing looping requires that _q_ is nonnegative. Hence a query is met in time (_d_+1)O(1)+O(1)=O(_d_).

**Correctness.** Let 1_,p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p<sub>h</sub>_ be the successive values _p_ is set to. In particular, \(h\le d\). The following properties hold:

• \(1<p_1<\dots<p_h\le n+1\);<tbc>

• for every \(i\in[h]\), \(w[(u-1)n+p_i-1]\neq w[(v-1)n+p_i-1]\);<tbc>

• for every \(j\in[p_h-1]\), if \(w[(u-1)n+j]\neq w[(v-1)n+j]\) then there exists \(i\in[h]\) such that _j=p<sub>i</sub>_-1.

The main invariant is that there are exactly _i_ vertices with label smaller than _p<sub>i</sub>_ adjacent to exactly one of _u,v_. As we check both if more than _d_ such positions where found (\(q\le 0\)) and if the current position overflows to the next adjacency vectors (\(p\le n\)), we correctly decide whether or not \(sd_G(u,v)\le d\) holds when exiting the while loop.

In particular, we can list _all_ pairs of _d_-near-twins in quadratic time, when _d_ is constant.

**Corollary 17.** _There is an_ O(_dn_<sup>2</sup>)_-time algorithm that, given an n-vertex graph and a positive integer d, lists all the pairs of vertices_ \(u,v\in V(G)\) _such that_ \(sd_G(u,v)\le d\).

_Proof._ We compute in O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time the data structure D of Theorem 16. For every \(u,v\in V(G)\) with \(u\neq v\), we present D with the query _u,v,d_. If the answer is positive (\(sd_G(u,v)\le d\)), we add _u,v_ to the output pairs. Overall, this takes O(_dn_<sup>2</sup>) time.

We obtain the objective of this section by repeatedly appling Corollary 17.

**Theorem 18.** _Let_ C _be a (hereditary) class of versatile symmetric difference of exponent_ \(\alpha\)_. There is an_ \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(n^{2+\alpha})\)_-time algorithm that, given an n-vertex graph of_ C_, outputs an sd-degeneracy sequence of G of width_ \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(n^\alpha)\).

_Proof._ Let _d_:=_d_<sub>C</sub>_\>_0 be such that for every _n_-vertex graph \(G\in\mathcal{C}\), there are \(\lfloor n/d\rfloor\) disjoint pairs of vertices _u,v_ satisfying \(\mathrm{sd}_G(u,v)\le dn^\alpha\). We initialize an sd-degeneracy sequence S of _G_ of width \(dn^\alpha\) to the empty list. We also set _G_<sub>1</sub>:=_G_ and _n_<sub>1</sub>:=_n_.

While the remaining graph _G<sub>i</sub>_ has \(n_i\ge d\) vertices, we do the following.

By Corollary 17, we list all the pairs of \(dn^\alpha\)-near-twins of _G<sub>i</sub>_ in \(\mathcal{O}(dn^\alpha n_i^2)\) time. We then greedily build a list {_u_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub>}_,...,{u<sub>h</sub>,v<sub>h</sub>_} of \(\mathrm{max}(1,\lfloor\frac{1}{2}\lfloor n_i/d\rfloor)\) _disjoint_ pairs of \(dn^\alpha\)-near-twins of _G<sub>i</sub>_ in O(_n<sub>i</sub>_) time. (Indeed, if one fixes a set _D_ disjoint pairs, then the choice of any other pair consumes at most two pairs of _D._) We append this list to S. We then set _G_<sub>_i_+1</sub>:=_G<sub>i</sub>_-{_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>h</sub>_} and _n_<sub>_i_+1</sub>:=|_V(G_<sub>_i_+1</sub>)|. This finishes the body of the while loop.

When we exit the while loop, we finish the sd-degeneracy sequence arbitrarily.

**Correctness.** If the algorithm terminates, it does output an sd-degeneracy sequence of _G_ of width \(dn^\alpha\) since we only append to S pairs of \(dn^\alpha\)-near-twins in the current graph, and remove their first elements in batches of disjoint pairs.

**Time.** At every loop iteration, we add at least one pair to the sequence and remove their first elements from the graph. Thus, the algorithm does terminate, and goes through the successive induced subgraphs of _G_: _G_<sub>1</sub>_,G_<sub>2</sub>_,...,G<sub>p</sub>_ with \(p\le n\). Let \(c:=1-\frac{1}{4d}\).

**Claim 19.** _For every_ \(i\in[p-1]\), \(n_{i+1}\le cn_i\).

_Proof._ Indeed, if _n<sub>i</sub>\<_4_d_, then \(n_{i+1}\le cn_i\) since \(n_{i+1}\le n_i-1\) (we remove at least one vertex of _G<sub>i</sub>_ to form _G_<sub>_i_+1</sub>). If instead, \(n_i\ge 4d\), we conclude because \(\mathrm{max}(1,\lfloor\frac{1}{2}\lfloor n_i/d\rfloor)=\lfloor\frac{1}{2}\lfloor n_i/d\rfloor\unknown\frac{1}{4d}\cdot n_i\).

By Claim 19, for every \(i\in[p]\), \(n_i\le c^{i-1}n\). So the overall running time is

\(\sum_{i\in[p]}\mathcal{O}(dn^\alpha n_i^2)\le\mathcal{O}(dn^\alpha)\cdot n^2\sum_{i\in[p]}c^{2i-2}\le\frac{1}{1-c}\cdot\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(n^{2+\alpha})=\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(n^{2+\alpha}),\)

and we conclude.

Theorem 3 is then a consequence of Theorems 18 and 33. For classes of bounded versatile symmetric difference (exponent 0), we get the following corollary (which, by Theorem 33, implies Theorem 1).

**Corollary 20.** _Let_ C _be a (hereditary) class of bounded versatile symmetric difference. There is an_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>)_-time algorithm that, given an n-vertex graph of_ C_, outputs an sd-degeneracy sequence of G of width_ O<sub>C</sub>(1).

## 4 SSSP in graphs given with an interval biclique partition

In this section we prove Theorem 5, which for convenience we recall below.

**Theorem 5.** _There is an_ O(_n+b)-time algorithm that, given an interval biclique partition of an n-vertex graph G with b bicliques and_ \(s\in V(G)\)_, outputs a shortest-path tree from vertex s in G._

We begin by introducing a data structure problem for reporting interval intersections, called Interval-Intersect, and we show how to solve this problem in total linear time. In Interval- Intersect, we are given as input a unary-encoded integer \(N\ge 1\) (the universe size) and a finite set _A_ of labels, where every label \(a\in A\) is assigned an integer interval \(I_a\subseteq[N]\). Initially, all labels are active. The data structure is required to answer the following online queries: given an integer interval \(J\subseteq[N]\), report all active labels \(a\in A\) with the corresponding intervals _I<sub>a</sub>_ intersecting _J_, and deactivate all reported labels.

Subsequently, we will use the resulting data structure to show the linear-time algorithm for Theorem 5. In Section 4.1, we prove the following.

**Lemma 21.** _There exists a data structure for Interval-Intersect in the word RAM model of computation that processes an instance with universe size N, set of labels A, and q queries in_ O(_N_+|_A_|+_q_) _time._

The purpose of encoding _N_ in unary is to ensure that every element of the universe \[_N_\] fits within a single RAM word; hence we can assume _N\<_2_<sup>b</sup>_ where _b_ is the size of the machine word.

We show now to use Lemma 21 to solve SSSP in linear time in graphs with a given interval biclique partition, namely, we prove Theorem 5.

_Proof of Theorem 5._ Recall that \[_n_\] is the vertex set of the graph, and let the _i_th biclique in the edge partition (\(i\in[b]\)) have sides _A<sub>i</sub>_ and _B<sub>i</sub>_; each _A<sub>i</sub>_ and _B<sub>i</sub>_ is a subinterval of \[_n_\].

In the beginning, we set up two instances of the linear-time data structure for Interval- Intersect, both with universe \[_n_\]:

• _D_gather, with labels from \[_n_\], where the label \(i\in[n]\) is assigned the interval \[_i,i_\];<tbc>

• _D_scatter, with labels \(\bigcup_{i\in[b]}\{a_i,b_i\}\), with the interval _A<sub>i</sub>_ assigned to _a<sub>i</sub>_ and the interval _B<sub>i</sub>_ assigned to _b<sub>i</sub>_.

The active items in _D_gather are the vertices undiscovered by the run of the breadth-first search (BFS); hence, we initially query _D_gather with \[_s,s_\], where _s_ is the source of the BFS, to deactivate the label _s_. On the other hand, the active items in _D_scatter represent the sides of the bicliques that do not contain vertices visited by BFS.

We perform the usual BFS in _G_, with the usual queue holding the vertices discovered by the search (initially only _s_) that are yet to be visited. When a vertex \(v\in[n]\) is visited by the search, we find the yet undiscovered neighbors of _v_ as follows. We first use _D_scatter to enumerate the not yet processed sides of the bicliques by querying _D_scatter for the interval \[_v,v_\]. Suppose _D_scatter returns _a<sub>i</sub>_ (resp., _b<sub>i</sub>_) as one of the labels; then, we have that \(v\in A_i\) (resp., \(v\in B_i\)). In this case, all vertices in _B<sub>i</sub>_ (resp., _A<sub>i</sub>_) should become discovered if not yet discovered. In order to ensure that, we query _D_gather with the interval _B<sub>i</sub>_ (resp., _A<sub>i</sub>_), and enqueue all vertices returned as a result of the query, marking _v_ as the parent of each of them. We repeat this process for each label reported by _D_scatter.

The correctness of the algorithm is clear as it is simply a breadth-first search with a bespoke method for listing the yet undiscovered neighbors. To see the efficiency, observe that we issue at most _n_ queries to _D_scatter, and it reports at most O(_b_) labels throughout the entire run of SSSP. Thus, at most O(_b_) queries to _D_gather are issued. Hence both data structures for Interval-Intersect process all respective queries in total O(_n+b_) time. Moreover, it is clear that outside of the queries, the SSSP implementation above takes time linear in the size of the input; the claim follows.

## 4.1 Interval intersections data structure

It remains to prove Lemma 21.

Our approach resembles the _tabulation technique_ and the _method of Four Russians_, commonly used in algorithm design in the word RAM model of computation; see e.g. \[3, 26, 8, 6\]. Namely, we first show a data structure with a worse complexity guarantee O(_N_log_N_+|_A_|+_q_) (Lemma 22). Using Lemma 22, we then show how to bootstrap a linear-time data structure for universes of size \(n\le N\), given access to a linear-time data structure for universes of size log_n_ (Lemma 23). Next, in the word RAM model, we give a linear-time data structure for universes of size \(\sqrt{logN}\), assuming O(_N_)-time prior preprocessing (Lemma 24). Applying Lemma 23 twice to Lemma 24 implies Lemma 21. We implement this strategy below.

**Lemma 22** (Quasi-linear interval intersections)**.** _There exists a data structure for Interval- Intersect that processes an instance with universe size N, set of labels A, and q queries in_ O(_N_log_N_+|_A_|+_q_) _time._

_Proof._ On initialization, we build an auxiliary directed graph _H_ with O(_N_log_N_+|_A_|) vertices and arcs, as follows. Let \(L=\lfloor logN\rfloor\). For integer \(k\in[0,L]\), let the _kth interval layer_ I_<sub>k</sub>_ comprise all integer intervals \([i,i+2^k-1]\subseteq[N]\). For every such _k_ and every interval \(I\in\mathcal{I}_k\), we introduce two vertices: an outvertex _u<sub>I</sub>_ and an invertex _v<sub>I</sub>_. For every \(a\in A\), we also introduce a vertex _a_.

We construct arcs in _H_ as follows. Every \(I\in\mathcal{I}_k\) with \(k\ge 1\) is a disjoint union of two integer intervals \(I_1,I_2\in\mathcal{I}_{k-1}\); add arcs \(u_I\rightarrow u_{I_1}\), \(u_I\rightarrow u_{I_2}\) (so that arcs between outvertices are directed toward lower-indexed layers) and arcs \(v_{I_1}\rightarrow v_I\), \(v_{I_2}\rightarrow v_I\) (so arcs between invvertices are oriented toward higher-indexed layers). Also, for every \(I=[i,i]\in\mathcal{I}_0\), add an arc \(u_I\rightarrow v_I\). It is easy to verify that now, for every \(I\in\mathcal{I}_k\) and \(x\in[N]\), there is a path from _u<sub>I</sub>_ to _u_<sub>\[_x,x_\]</sub> if and only if \(x\in I\); and by the same token, there is a path from _v_<sub>\[_x,x_\]</sub> to _v<sub>I</sub>_ if and only if \(x\in I\). It follows that for an outvertex _u<sub>J</sub>_ and an invertex _v<sub>I</sub>_, a path from _u<sub>J</sub>_ to _v<sub>I</sub>_ exists if and only if the intervals _J_ and _I_ intersect. Finally, for every \(a\in A\) with the corresponding interval _I<sub>a</sub>_, write _I<sub>a</sub>_ as a (not necessarily disjoint) union of two intervals \(I_1,I_2\in\mathcal{I}_k\) for some \(k\in[0,L]\) (where possibly _I_<sub>1</sub>=_I_<sub>2</sub>). Then add arcs \(v_{I_1}\rightarrow a\), \(v_{I_2}\rightarrow a\). This guarantees that for any outvertex _u<sub>J</sub>_, a path from _u<sub>J</sub>_ to _a_ in _H_ exists if and only if _J_ and _I<sub>a</sub>_ intersect. See Fig. 4.

Apart from the graph _H_, we also initialize a visited bit vis_<sub>v</sub>_ for each \(v\in V(H)\), initially unset. Then consider a query _J_. As above, write _J_ as a union of two intervals \(J_1,J_2\in\mathcal{I}_k\) for some \(k\in[0,L]\). Then perform two graph searches in _H_ from the outvertices _u_<sub>_J_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,u_<sub>_J_<sub>2</sub></sub>, visiting only previously unvisited vertices of _H_, and marking these vertices as visited. For each newly visited vertex \(a\in A\), we report _a_ as the label corresponding to the interval _I<sub>a</sub>_ intersecting _J_.

The correctness of the data structure is clear. For the efficiency of the data structure, observe that _H_ has size O(_N_log_N_+|_A_|) and can be constructed in time proportional to its size. Then, each of the _q_ queries spawns at most two graph searches in _H_ that only visit previously unvisited vertices. Therefore, all queries are processed in total time O(_N_log_N_+|_A_|+_q_), as required.

We then show how to use Lemma 22 to bootstrap a data structure for tiny universes to handle an exponentially larger universe. In the next lemma, _b_ is the size of the machine word.

**Lemma 23** (Bootstrapping for interval intersections)**.** _Let N_max_\<_2_<sup>b</sup> be an integer. Suppose there exists a data structure for Interval-Intersect that processes instances with universe of size_ \(N\le logN_\mathrm{max}\)_, set of labels A, and q queries in_ O(_N_+|_A_|+_q_) _time. Then there exists a data structure for Interval-Intersect that processes instances with universe of size_ \(N\le N_\mathrm{max}\)_, the set of labels A, and q queries in_ O(_N_+|_A_|+_q) time._

_Proof._ We construct the promised data structure as follows. Let \(\ell=max(1,\lfloor logN\rfloor)\) and partition \[_N_\] into \(m=\lceil\frac{N}{\ell}\rceil\) blocks _B_<sub>1</sub>_,...,B<sub>m</sub>_ of length \(\ell\); the last block is shorter if needed. For an interval \(I\subseteq[N]\), define:

• \(\text{inter}(I)\subseteq[m]\) to be the (nonempty) interval of indices of blocks that intersect _I_;<tbc>

• \(\text{core}(I)\subseteq[m]\) to be the (possibly empty) interval of indices of blocks that are fully contained within _I_;<tbc>

• fringe(_I_) to be the collection (of size at most 2) of nonempty intervals \(I\cap B_i\) over all blocks \(i\in\text{inter}(I)\backslash\text{core}(I)\).

Also, whenever _I_ is a subinterval of _B<sub>i</sub>_, let \(\text{rel}_i(I)\subseteq[\ell]\) be the position of the interval _I_ relative to _B<sub>i</sub>_, i.e., the interval _I_ with both endpoints shifted by \(-(i-1)\ell\).

## Correctness.

Let _I<sub>a</sub>_ be an input interval labeled _a_ and _J_ be a query interval. First, suppose _a_ is reported by the query. Then, _a_ was still active before the query. If _D_<sub>core</sub> reported _a_, then \(\mathsf{core}(I_a)\cap\mathsf{inter}(J)\neq\emptyset\), which easily implies \(I_a\cap J\neq\emptyset\). Next, if _D_<sub>fringe</sub> reported _a_, then a fringe subinterval \(I'\in\mathsf{fringe}(I_a)\) resides in a block belonging to core(_J_); hence \(I'\cap J\neq\emptyset\) and so \(I_a\cap J\neq\emptyset\). Finally, if _a_ is returned by _D<sub>i</sub>_, then there exist \(I'\in\mathsf{fringe}(I_a)\) and \(J'\in\mathsf{fringe}(J)\), both within the _i_th block, so that \(I'\cap J'\neq\emptyset\); hence trivially \(I_a\cap J\neq\emptyset\).

Conversely, suppose \(I_a\cap J\neq\emptyset\) and _a_ is active. Let _x_ be any element of the intersection and suppose _x_ is within the _i_th block. First, if \(i\in\mathsf{core}(I_a)\), then _D_<sub>core</sub> definitely reports _a_ since _J_ intersects the _i_th block. Otherwise, \(x\in I'\) for some \(I'\in\mathsf{fringe}(I_a)\). If \(i\in\mathsf{core}(J)\), then _D_<sub>fringe</sub> reports _a_ as the data structure carries the interval \[_i,i_\] labeled _a_. In the opposite case, \(x\in J'\) for some \(J'\in\mathsf{fringe}(J)\) and so \(I'\cap J'\neq\emptyset\). Therefore, _D<sub>i</sub>_ returns _a_. We conclude that an active label _a_ is output if and only if \(I_a\cap J\neq\emptyset\), which implies the correctness of our implementation.

## Time.

Suppose _q_ queries are processed by our data structure. Both _D_<sub>core</sub> and _D_<sub>fringe</sub> maintain a universe of size _m_, hold at most O(|_A_|) labels, and accept at most _q_ queries. Thus both of these auxiliary data structures initialize and process the queries in total time O(_m_log_m_+|_A_|+_q_)=O(_N_+|_A_|+_q_). Then, the data structures _D<sub>i</sub>_ have total universe size \(m\ell=\mathcal{O}(N)\), carry at most O(|_A_|) labels in total, and accept O(_q_) queries in total. By our assumption, they all process all the queries in total time O(_N_+|_A_|+_q_). Therefore, the time complexity of our constructed data structure is also linear.

Then, whenever _a<sub>i</sub>_ is reported by _D_<sub>fringe</sub>, we translate the label _a<sub>i</sub>_ to _a_ on the fly.

Note that in Lemma 23, the constant hidden in the O notation of the resulting data structure is greater than the constant hidden in the prerequisite data structure.

It remains to give a linear-time data structure for sufficiently small universe sizes.

**Lemma 24** (Efficient interval intersections for tiny universes)**.** _Let b be the size of the machine word and_ \(\ell\le\sqrt{b}\)_. There exists a data structure for any instance of Interval-Intersect with the universe size at most_ \(\ell\) _that takes a finite set A of labels and processes q queries in total time_ \(\mathcal{O}(\ell+|A|+q)\)_. The data structure requires a global table, which can be computed given only_ \(\ell\) _in time_ \(\mathcal{O}(2^{\ell^2})\).

_Proof._ Fix \(\ell\) as the universe size; if the universe size of an instance is smaller than \(\ell\), we can artificially increase it to \(\ell\). Define the _state_ of an instance of Interval-Intersect to be the set of _active_ integer intervals of \([\ell]\): the intervals assigned to the active labels of the instance. Note that there are exactly \(2^{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell+1}{2}}\) different states since there are \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell+1}{2}\) integer subintervals of \([\ell]\). We represent states in memory as bitmasks of length \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell+1}{2}\); this is permitted in our computation model as \(b\ge\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell+1}{2}\).

In the preprocessing stage, we initialize a global two-dimensional table _T_ as follows. For a state _S_ and an interval \(J\subseteq[\ell]\), we define _T_\[_S_\]\[_J_\]=(_S_in_,S_out), where _S_in is the set of intervals of _S_ intersecting _J_, and _S_out is the remaining intervals of _S_. Observe that when an instance of Interval-Intersect is in state _S_, then performing a query _J_ on it transitions it to state _S_out and returns all labels with the corresponding intervals in _S_in. Let also, for a state _S_ and an interval \(I\in S\), the value _F_\[_S_\]\[_I_\] be an integer such that, for each _S_, the mapping from intervals \(I\in S\) to the values _F_\[_S_\]\[_I_\] is a bijection between _S_ and \(\lfloor|S|\rfloor\). We also explicitly compute an \(\mathcal{O}(\ell^2)\)-sized array _M_ mapping integer subintervals of \([\ell]\) to their bit index within the state. The arrays can be constructed in time \(2^{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{\ell+1}{2}}\ell^{\mathcal{O}(1)}\in\mathcal{O}(2^{\ell^2})\).

We now give an implementation of the data structure. On initialization, we compute the initial state _S_init from \(\ell\) and _A_ using _M_. Then create buckets _B_<sub>1</sub>_,...,B_<sub>|_S_init|</sub> of labels from _A_, and for each label \(a\in A\), insert _a_--corresponding to an interval \(I_a\in S_\text{init}\)--into bucket _B_<sub>_F_\[_S_init\]\[_I<sub>a</sub>_\]</sub>. This can be done in total \(\mathcal{O}(\ell+|A|)\) time. Let also _S_ track the current state of the data structure; initially _S=S_init. Then, for a given query _J_, let (_S_in_,S_out)=_T_\[_S_\]\[_J_\]. We update the state of the data structure to _S_out and return all labels of the intervals in _S_in (i.e., all labels in the buckets _B_<sub>_F_\[_S_init\]\[_I_\]</sub> for \(I\in S_\text{in}\)). This can clearly be done in time O(1+_t_), where _t_ denotes the total number of returned labels. Therefore, all queries are processed in total time \(\mathcal{O}(\ell+|A|+q)\).

Given Lemmas 23 and 24, the proof of Lemma 21 is direct.

_Proof of Lemma 21._ Fix the universe size _N\<_2_<sup>b</sup>_, and let \(\ell=max(1,\lceil loglogN\rceil)\). By Lemma 24, after preprocessing in time \(\mathcal{O}(2^{\ell^2})=o(N)\), we can construct a data structure for Interval- Intersect processing instances with a universe of size at most \(\ell\), the set of labels _A_, and _q_ queries in time \(\mathcal{O}(\ell+|A|+q)\). Applying Lemma 23 the first time with \(N_{max}=2^\ell\), we get a data structure for universes of size \(n\le 2^\ell\) with total time O(_n_+|_A_|+_q_). Applying Lemma 23 once again with _N_max=_N_, we end with the required data structure.

## 6 Finding an sd-degeneracy sequence in randomized linear time

In this section, we prove Theorem 4: we show how to compute an sd-degeneracy sequence of width \(\mathcal{O}(n^{1-1/\rho})\) in expected linear time in graphs of VC density \(\rho\). In particular, this yields an expected linear-time algorithm that outputs sd-degeneracy sequences of constant width in classes of linear neighborhood complexity (Theorem 2). The proof relies on a result in learning theory and VC- combinatorics related to Haussler’s packing lemma (Theorem 32).

A _set system_ on a domain _D_ is a set F of subsets of _D_. For \(A\subseteq D\), denote<tbc>

\(\mathcal{F}\unknown_A:=\{F\cap A:F\in\mathcal{F}\}.\)

<tbc>The _shatter function_ of a set system F is the function \(\pi_\mathcal{F}:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}\) defined by

\(\pi_\mathcal{F}(m):=max\{|\mathcal{F}\unknown_A|:A\subseteq D,|A|\le m\}.\)

The _VC dimension_ of a set system F is the largest integer _d_ such that there exists a subset \(A\subseteq D\) of size _d_ with F\(\unknown_A=2^A\).

Given a finite domain _X_, an _s-sample_ is a tuple \(S=(x_1,\dots,x_s)\in X^s\) of _s_ elements of _X_. We will consider _s_-samples of _X_ drawn uniformly at random, that is, each element _x<sub>i</sub>_ of _S_ is drawn independently and uniformly at random from _X_. (Note that an _s_-sample can contain the same element multiple times.)

Given a set _F_ and an _s_-sample _S_=(_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>s</sub>_), denote \(F\cap S:=F\cap\{x_1,\dots,x_s\}\). For a set system F on a domain _X_ and integer \(s\ge 1\), denote

\(\mathcal{F}\unknown_s:=\{(S,F\cap S)|S\in X^s,F\in\mathcal{F}\},\)

that is, the set of all restrictions of sets in F to all possible samples of size _s_. The next lemma originates in \[38, Lemma 9\] as part of a proof of Haussler’s packing lemma. It is in the spirit of the classical PAC learning model, and states that sets from a set system of bounded VC dimension can be learned from a small random sample.

**Lemma 25** (\[38\])**.** _Let_ F _be a set system on a finite domain X of VC dimension at most d. For any_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _and integer_ \(s\ge 1\)_, there exists a map_ \(f:\mathcal{F}\unknown_s\rightarrow 2^X\) _such that for every_ \(F\in\mathcal{F}\),

\(\mathbb{P}_{S\sim X^s}\left(|F\triangle f(S,F\cap S)|<\frac{d}{\varepsilon s}\cdot|X|\right)\ge 1-\varepsilon,\)

_where S∼X<sup>s</sup> denotes that S is an s-sample of X, drawn uniformly at random._

The next algorithm relies on the existence of the map _f_ as above, but does not require to compute it explicitly.

**Lemma 26.** _Fix real numbers_ \(c,\rho\ge 1\) _and_ \(\delta>0\)_, and let_ \(\alpha:=1-1/\rho\)_. There is a Las Vegas randomized algorithm that, given an n-vertex graph G with_ \((c,\rho)\)_-polynomial neighborhood complexity and a set_ \(U\subseteq V(G)\) _with_ \(|U|\ge max(\delta n,2)\)_, outputs in expected time_

\(\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho,\delta}\left(n+\sum_{u\in U}deg_G(u)\right)\)

_a set of_ \(\Omega_{c,\rho,\delta}(|U|)\) _disjoint pairs of_ \(\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho,\delta}(n^\alpha)\)_-near-twins contained in U._

_Proof._ We may assume that \(\delta\le 1\). If \(|U|<2^{\rho+1}c\), then \(n\le|U|/\delta=\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho,\delta}(1)\). An arbitrary maximal pairing of _U_ has size at least |_U|/_4, and every pair has symmetric difference at most \(n=\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho,\delta}(n^\alpha)\), so we are done. Henceforth assume that \(|U|\ge 2^{\rho+1}c\).

We first consider the case when _U_ contains no pair of vertices which are twins in _G_. Let<tbc>

\(\mathcal{F}:=\{N_G(u)|u\in U\}\)

<tbc>be the set system with domain _V(G_) of neighborhoods of vertices of _U_. The members of F are distinct, and, since _G_ has \((c,\rho)\)-polynomial neighborhood complexity,<tbc>

\(\pi_\mathcal{F}(m)\le\pi_G(m)\le c\cdot m^\rho\)

<tbc>for every positive integer _m_. Let _d_<sub>0</sub> be the VC dimension of F. Since \(|\mathcal{F}|=|U|\ge 2\), we have \(d_0\ge 1\), and

\(2^{d_0}\le\pi_\mathcal{F}(d_0)\le c\cdot d_0^\rho.\)

Consequently, there is an integer \(d:=d(c,\rho)\), fixed independently of the input, such that \(d_0\le d\).

Let<tbc>

\(s:=\left[\left(\frac{|U|}{2c}\right)^{1/\rho}\right],\varepsilon:=\frac{1}{16},k:=\left\lceil\frac{2dn}{\varepsilon s}\right\rceil.\)

<tbc>Our lower bound on |_U_| ensures that<tbc>

\(s\ge\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{|U|}{2c}\right)^{1/\rho}\text{and}cs^\rho\le\frac{|U|}{2}.\)

<tbc>Moreover,<tbc>

\(k\le 1+\frac{4dn(2c)^{1/\rho}}{\varepsilon|U|^{1/\rho}}\le\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho,\delta}\left(n^{1-\frac{1}{\rho}}\right).\)

<tbc>Fix a map _f_ as in Lemma 25, using the upper bound _d_ on the VC dimension. For an _s_-sample _S_, we call an element \(F\in\mathcal{F}\) _bad_ (with respect to _S_) if<tbc>

\(|F\triangle f(S,F\cap S)|\ge\frac{k}{2}.\)

<tbc>By Lemma 25, for any fixed \(F\in\mathcal{F}\), the probability over the random choice of _S_ that _F_ is bad is at most \(\varepsilon\). Thus, the expected number of bad elements of F is at most \(\varepsilon|U|\). By Markov’s inequality,<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}_{S\sim V(G)^s}\left(|\{F\in\mathcal{F}|F\text{is bad with respect to}S\}|>|U|/8\right)\le\frac{\varepsilon|U|}{|U|/8}=8\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2}.\)

One attempt of the algorithm draws an _s_-sample _S_ of _V(G_) and lets \(\widehat{S}\subseteq V(G)\) be its underlying set. Consider the set system<tbc>

\(\mathcal{F}\unknown_\widehat{S}:=\{N_G(u)\cap\widehat{S}|u\in U\}.\)

<tbc>We have

\(|\mathcal{F}\unknown_\widehat{S}|\le\pi_\mathcal{F}(|\widehat{S}|)\le c|\widehat{S}|^\rho\le cs^\rho\le\frac{|U|}{2}.\)

For each \(\widehat{F}\in\mathcal{F}\unknown_\widehat{S}\), let the _bucket_ \(B(\widehat{F})\) be the set of sets \(F\in\mathcal{F}\) such that \(F\cap\widehat{S}=\widehat{F}\). Thus, the buckets partition F.

Inside every bucket, we arbitrarily choose a maximum set of pairwise disjoint pairs, leaving at most one set unpaired. Let P be the collection of pairs obtained from all the buckets, and let \(\mathcal{P}_\text{good}\subseteq\mathcal{P}\) consist of those pairs {_F_<sub>1</sub>_,F_<sub>2</sub>} such that \(|F_1\triangle F_2|\le k\). If \(|\mathcal{P}_\text{good}|\ge|U|/8\), we output the corresponding pairs of vertices in _U_; otherwise, we discard the attempt and resample _S_.

**Claim 27.** _One attempt takes expected time_ \(\mathcal{O}(n+\sum_{u\in U}deg_G(u))\).

_Proof of claim._ Sampling _S_ takes O(_n_) time. Computing \(\mathcal{F}\unknown_\widehat{S}\) and partitioning F into buckets takes expected time \(\mathcal{O}(n+\sum_{u\in U}deg_G(u))\) by scanning the adjacency lists of the vertices in _U_. Building the candidate pairs takes O(|_U_|) time.

Given a candidate pair {_F_<sub>1</sub>_,F_<sub>2</sub>}, computing \(F_1\triangle F_2\) takes O(|_F_<sub>1</sub>|+|_F_<sub>2</sub>|) time. As the candidate pairs are disjoint, checking all of them takes \(\mathcal{O}(|U|+\sum_{u\in U}deg_G(u))\) time. \(\lrcorner\)

**Claim 28.** _Every attempt succeeds with probability at least_ 1/2.

_Proof of claim._ Let _F_<sub>1</sub>_,F_<sub>2</sub> lie in the same bucket. Then \(F_1\cap S=F_2\cap S\), and hence

\(|F_1\triangle F_2|\le|F_1\triangle f(S,F_1\cap S)|+|F_2\triangle f(S,F_2\cap S)|.\)

Therefore, every pair in P\\P<sub>good</sub> contains a bad element of F. As the candidate pairs are disjoint, the number of such pairs is at most the number of bad elements.

If the buckets are _B_<sub>1</sub>_,...,B<sub>t</sub>_, then \(t=|\mathcal{F}\unknown_\widehat{S}|\le|U|/2\) and<tbc>

\(|\mathcal{P}|=\sum_{j=1}^t\left\lfloor\frac{|B_j|}{2}\right\rfloor\ge\frac{|U|-t}{2}\ge\frac{|U|}{4}.\)

<tbc>With probability at least 1/2, at most |_U|/_8 elements of F are bad, and on that event

\(|\mathcal{P}_\text{good}|\ge|\mathcal{P}|-\frac{|U|}{8}\ge\frac{|U|}{8}.\)

Thus, the attempt succeeds. \(\lrcorner\)

The expected number of attempts is at most two, so Claim 27 proves the claimed expected running time when _U_ contains no pair of twins in _G_.

In the general case, construct a graph \(G'\) by adding, for every \(u\in U\), a new private pendant vertex _x<sub>u</sub>_ adjacent only to _u_. Then the vertices of _U_ have pairwise distinct neighborhoods in \(G'\). We claim that \(G'\) has \((c+2,\rho)\)-polynomial neighborhood complexity. Indeed, fix a nonempty set \(A\subseteq V(G')\), and put \(A_0:=A\cap V(G)\) and _A_<sub>1</sub>:=_A_\\_V(G_). The traces of the old vertices are determined by their traces on _A_<sub>0</sub>, except that at most |_A_<sub>1</sub>| of them can acquire a private pendant<tbc>

element. The new pendant vertices have traces among \(\emptyset\) and the singletons {_u_} for \(u\in A_0\). Consequently, the total number of traces on _A_ is at most

\(c|A|^\rho+|A|+1\le(c+2)|A|^\rho.\)

Also, \(|V(G')|\le 2n\), \(|U|\ge(\delta/2)|V(G')|\), and \(\mathrm{deg}_{G^\prime}(u)=\mathrm{deg}_G(u)+1\) for every \(u\in U\). We can therefore apply the twin-free case to \(G'\) and _U_ with constants _c_+2, \(\rho\), and \(\delta/2\). This application has the claimed expected running time. Finally, deleting the new pendant vertices cannot increase a symmetric difference, so the returned pairs satisfy the asserted bound in _G_ as well.

We now present the randomized linear-time algorithm computing an sd-degeneracy sequence.

**Theorem 4.** _For every real number_ \(\rho\ge 1\) _and every graph class_ C _of VC density_ \(\rho\)_, there is a randomized algorithm that, given a graph_ \(G\in\mathcal{C}\)_, outputs an sd-degeneracy sequence of G of width_ \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(n^{1-\frac{1}{\rho}})\) _in expected time_ \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}\big(|V(G)|+|E(G)|\big)\).

_Proof._ Let \(c\ge 1\) be such that every graph in C has \((c,\rho)\)-polynomial neighborhood complexity. Write _n_:=|_V(G_)|, _m_:=|_E(G_)|, and \(\alpha:=1-1/\rho\). We build a sequence _G_<sub>1</sub>_,G_<sub>2</sub>_,..._ of induced subgraphs of _G_, with _G_<sub>1</sub>:=_G_. Every _G<sub>i</sub>_ still has \((c,\rho)\)-polynomial neighborhood complexity.

In every iteration _i_ with \(n_i:=|V(G_i)|\ge 3\), let \(U_i\subseteq V(G_i)\) be the set of \(\lceil n_i/2\rceil\) vertices of _G<sub>i</sub>_ with smallest degrees, breaking ties arbitrarily. By Lemma 26, applied to _G<sub>i</sub>_, _U<sub>i</sub>_, and \(\delta=1/2\), in expected time

\(\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}\left(n_i+\sum_{u\in U_i}\mathrm{deg}_{G_i}(u)\right)\)

we find a set P_<sub>i</sub>_ of \(\Omega_{c,\rho}(n_i)\) disjoint pairs of \(\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}(n_i^\alpha)\)-near-twins inside _U<sub>i</sub>_. We order every pair of P_<sub>i</sub>_ arbitrarily, append the ordered pairs to the output sequence, and obtain _G_<sub>_i_+1</sub> by deleting the first vertex of every pair. When at most two vertices remain, we append their pair if there are two vertices, and terminate.

**Claim 29.** _The output is an sd-degeneracy sequence of G of width_ \(\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}(n^\alpha)\).

_Proof of claim._ Consider a pair (_u,v_) from a batch P_<sub>i</sub>_ when it is reached in the output sequence. Earlier pairs of the same batch are vertex-disjoint from (_u,v_), and the graph then present is an induced subgraph of _G<sub>i</sub>_. Hence, its symmetric difference is no larger than it was in _G<sub>i</sub>_, where (_u,v_) is a pair of \(\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}(n_i^\alpha)\)-near-twins. Since \(n_i\le n\), this is \(\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}(n^\alpha)\). If the algorithm terminates with two vertices, their symmetric difference is at most 2, and hence at most \(2n^\alpha\). \(\lrcorner\)

**Claim 30.** _The expected running time is_ \(\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}(n+m)\).

_Proof of claim._ We maintain deg<sub>_G<sub>i</sub>_</sub>(_v_) for every current vertex _v_, initialized in O(_n+m_) time. When vertices are deleted, we update the degrees of their surviving neighbors; all such updates cost O(_n+m_) in total. In iteration _i_, a linear-time selection algorithm applied to these maintained degrees finds the \(\lceil n_i/2\rceil\) vertices of smallest degree in O(_n<sub>i</sub>_) time.

By conditional linearity of expectation, the remaining expected work is bounded by

\(\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}\left(\sum_in_i+\sum_i\sum_{u\in U_i}\mathrm{deg}_{G_i}(u)\right).\) (1)

<tbc>Every iteration removes \(\Omega_{c,\rho}(n_i)\) vertices. Thus, the sequence (_n<sub>i</sub>)<sub>i</sub>_ decreases geometrically, and<tbc>

\(\sum_in_i=\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}(n).\)

<tbc>For the second term of (1), we have<tbc>

\(\sum_i\sum_{u\in U_i}\mathrm{deg}_{G_i}(u)=\sum_{r\ge 1}|S_r|,\text{with}S_r:=\{(i,u)|u\in U_i\text{and}\mathrm{deg}_{G_i}(u)\ge r\}.\)

<tbc>For every _r_ with \(S_r\neq\emptyset\), let _i<sub>r</sub>_ be the smallest index such that _U<sub>i<sub>r</sub></sub>_ contains a vertex of degree at least _r_. The geometric decrease and \(|U_i|=\Theta(n_i)\) imply<tbc>

\(|S_r|\le\sum_{i\ge i_r}|U_i|=\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}(|U_{i_r}|).\)

<tbc>For every \(r\ge 1\), let<tbc>

\(A_r:=\{v\in V(G)|\mathrm{deg}_G(v)\ge r\}.\)

<tbc>Because _U<sub>i<sub>r</sub></sub>_ consists of the lower half of the degree order and contains a vertex of degree at least _r_, every vertex of _V(G<sub>i<sub>r</sub></sub>_)\\_U<sub>i<sub>r</sub></sub>_ has degree at least _r_ in _G<sub>i<sub>r</sub></sub>_, and hence also in _G_. Therefore,<tbc>

\(\left\lfloor\frac{n_{i_r}}{2}\right\rfloor\le|A_r|\text{and consequently}|U_{i_r}|\le|A_r|+1.\)

<tbc>Since \(S_r=\emptyset\) for \(r\ge n\) and \(\sum_{r\ge 1}|A_r|=2m\), we obtain

\(\sum_i\sum_{u\in U_i}\mathrm{deg}_{G_i}(u)=\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}|S_r|\le\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}\left(\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}(|A_r|+1)\right)=\mathcal{O}_{c,\rho}(n+m).\)

Substituting both estimates into (1) proves the claim. \(\lrcorner\)

We conclude by Claims 29 and 30.

## 7 Finding Small Patterns

We next design a randomized linear-time algorithm that returns a triangle (if one exists) in graphs from a class of linear neighborhood complexity. The main idea is to use an sd-degeneracy sequence of the input graph to guide the search. In the next three (almost-)linear algorithms we assume that the edges of the input graph are preprocessed into a static dictionary in O(_n+m_) expected time and O(_n+m_) space, supporting adjacency queries in O(1) expected time.

**Theorem 8.** _For every graph class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity, Triangle Detection can be solved in expected time_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n+m_) _on n-vertex m-edge graphs of_ C.

_Proof._ Let _G_ be any input graph. By Theorem 2, we get an sd-degeneracy sequence (_u_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,(u_<sub>_n_-1</sub>_,v_<sub>_n_-1</sub>) of _G_ of width _d_=O<sub>C</sub>(1) in randomized time O<sub>C</sub>(_n+m_).

For every \(i\in[n-1]\), we define _G<sub>i</sub>_:=_G_-{_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u_<sub>_i_-1</sub>}. Note that to find a triangle in _G=G_<sub>1</sub> (if any), it is enough to return a triangle of _G_<sub>1</sub> that contains _u_<sub>1</sub> or obtain the guarantee that _not_ all the triangles of _G_<sub>1</sub> contain _u_<sub>1</sub>, and recursively apply this strategy to _G_<sub>2</sub>. Indeed, at each step we either find a triangle in _G<sub>i</sub>_ or move to _G_<sub>_i_+1</sub> with the promise that _G_<sub>_i_+1</sub> contains a triangle if and only if _G<sub>i</sub>_ contains one.

We set

\(A_i:=N_{G_i}(u_i)\backslash N_{G_i}(v_i)\text{and}X_i:=N_{G_i}(u_i)\cap N_{G_i}(v_i)\)

for every \(i\in[n-1]\).

For _i_ going from 1 to _n_-2, the algorithm proceeds as follows. Compute _A<sub>i</sub>_ in time O(|_N<sub>G<sub>i</sub></sub>(u<sub>i</sub>_)|) by filtering out the vertices of _N<sub>G<sub>i</sub></sub>(u<sub>i</sub>_) that are adjacent to _v<sub>i</sub>_. By assumption, \(|A_i|\le d\). For every \(a\in A_i\) and every \(b\in N_{G_i}(u_i)\) check if \(ab\in E(G_i)\). If so, return the triangle _u<sub>i</sub>ab_ (break from the for loop, and terminate). Even if all the checks are unsuccessful, this takes \(\mathcal{O}\left((d+1)\cdot|N_{G_i}(u_i)|\right)\) time. If no triangle is found, remove _u<sub>i</sub>_ from _G<sub>i</sub>_ in time O(|_N<sub>G<sub>i</sub></sub>(u<sub>i</sub>_)|) to obtain _G_<sub>_i_+1</sub> (and move to the next iteration of the for loop).

**Correctness.** If there is a triangle in _G<sub>i</sub>_ that contains _u<sub>i</sub>_ but the algorithm does not return one at the _i_th iteration of the for loop, it is of the form _u<sub>i</sub>xy_ with \(\{x,y\}\subseteq X_i\). Then _G_<sub>_i_+1</sub> still contains at least the triangle _v<sub>i</sub>xy_.

**Running time.** Computing the sd-degeneracy sequences takes randomized time O<sub>C</sub>(_n+m_). The rest of the algorithm takes time

\(\mathcal{O}\left(\sum_{i\in[n-2]}(d+1)\cdot(|N_{G_i}(u_i)|+1)\right)=\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(n+m).\)

We now build on the scheme of the previous proof to detect a 4-vertex clique. The randomized almost linear algorithm relies on both an sd-degeneracy sequence _and_ a Welzl order.

**Theorem 9.** _For every graph class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity, a K_<sub>4</sub> _subgraph can be found in expected_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_log<sup>5</sup>_n+m_log_n_) _or in deterministic_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>) _time on n-vertex m-edge graphs of_ C.

_Proof._ We obtain an sd-degeneracy sequence (_u_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,(u_<sub>_n_-1</sub>_,v_<sub>_n_-1</sub>) of the input graph _G_ of width _d_=O<sub>C</sub>(1) in randomized O<sub>C</sub>(_n+m_) time by Theorem 2, or deterministic O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time by Theorem 1. For every \(i\in[n-1]\), we define _G<sub>i</sub>,A<sub>i</sub>,X<sub>i</sub>_ as in the proof of Theorem 8.

Our general strategy remains the same. Now, for every \(a\in A_i\), we do not merely need to know if \(Z_{i,a}\neq\emptyset\) but rather whether _G<sub>i</sub>_\[_Z<sub>i,a</sub>_\] contains an edge, where

\(Z_{i,a}:=N_{G_i}(u_i)\cap N_{G_i}(a).\)

We start describing the deterministic O(_n_<sup>2</sup>)-time algorithm, which naturally uses Theorem 1 as opening step.

Let _M_ be an arbitrary adjacency matrix of _G_, on which we compute the data structure of Theorem 7 (associated sparse matrix) in O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time. For _i_ going from 1 to _n_-3, the algorithm proceeds as follows. It computes _A<sub>i</sub>_ in time O(|_N<sub>G<sub>i</sub></sub>(u<sub>i</sub>_)|). For every \(a\in A_i\), it computes the indicator (column) vector _z<sub>i,a</sub>_ of _Z<sub>i,a</sub>_ in time O(_n_).

We observe that

\(z_{i,a}^TMz_{i,a}=2|E(G_i[Z_{i,a}])|,\)

and compute the matrix-vector product _y<sub>i,a</sub>_:=_Mz<sub>i,a</sub>_ in time O<sub>C</sub>(_n_), by Theorem 7. We now check in O(_n_) time whether there is a \(j\in[n]\) such that both _z<sub>i,a</sub>_\[_j_\] and _y<sub>i,a</sub>_\[_j_\] are nonzero. If this happens, we know that there is at least one edge in _G<sub>i</sub>_\[_Z<sub>i,a</sub>_\] incident to the _j_th vertex, say _x_, of _G_. We can find the other endpoint of such an edge, say _y_, in O(_n_) time. We return the 4-vertex clique {_u<sub>i</sub>,a,x,y_} (and terminate).

If no _K_<sub>4</sub> is found, we remove _u<sub>i</sub>_ from _G<sub>i</sub>_ in time O(|_N<sub>G<sub>i</sub></sub>(u<sub>i</sub>_)|) to obtain _G_<sub>_i_+1</sub> (and move to the next iteration of the for loop). This concludes the algorithm.

Each iteration takes O((_d_+1)_n_)=O<sub>C</sub>(_n_) time because \(|A_i|\le d\). The preprocessing of _M_ takes O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time. Therefore, the overall running time is O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>). The correctness follows as in the proof of Theorem 8.

We now describe the randomized O<sub>C</sub>(_n_log<sup>5</sup>_n+m_log_n_)-time algorithm, which first calls Theorem 2. In addition to the sd-degeneracy sequence, we will rely on a Welzl order for _G_; more specifically, in time O<sub>C</sub>((_n+m_)log_n_) we compute a vertex ordering \(\prec\): _w_<sub>1</sub>_w_<sub>2</sub>_...w<sub>n</sub>_ such that the neighborhood of every vertex of _G_ is the union of \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(\mathrm{log}^2n)\prec\)-intervals \[23\]. We further compute, for every \(v\in V(G)\), the \(\prec\)-intervals _I_<sub>1</sub>(_v),...,I<sub>h<sub>v</sub></sub>(v_) with _h<sub>v</sub>_=O<sub>C</sub>(log<sup>2</sup>_n_) such that \(N_G(v)=\unknown_{j\in[h_v]}I_j(v)\); overall this takes time O(_n+m_). We observe that the orderings _u_<sub>1</sub>_u_<sub>2</sub>_..._ and _w_<sub>1</sub>_w_<sub>2</sub>_..._ are a priori unrelated. For every \(v\in V(G)\), we denote by \(\pi(v)\) the integer _i_ such that _v=w<sub>i</sub>_.

We create the following planar point set _P_, with |_P_|=2_m_. For every \(uv\in E(G)\), we add points \((\pi(u),\pi(v))\) and \((\pi(v),\pi(u))\) to _P_. In O(_m_log_n_) preprocessing time, a data structure D_<sub>P</sub>_ can be computed that answers rectangle query (given an axis-parallel rectangle _R_, yield a point in \(R\cap P\)) in time O(log_n_) \[20, Theorem 2\].

Let<tbc>

\(\widehat{Z}_{i,a}:=N_G(u_i)\cap N_G(a),\)

<tbc>and note the _G_ subscripts (so in particular \(\widehat{Z}_{i,a}\supseteq Z_{i,a}\)). We proceed as the deterministic O<sub>C</sub>(_n_<sup>2</sup>)- time algorithm, except we decide if \(G[\widehat{Z}_{i,a}]\) (not _G<sub>i</sub>_\[_Z<sub>i,a</sub>_\]) has an edge with the \(\prec\)-intervals _I<sub>j</sub>(v_) and D_<sub>P</sub>_. (We do not compute _M_ nor _z<sub>i,a</sub>_.) We compute \(\widehat{Z}_{i,a}\) as the intersection of

\(\unknown_{j\in[h_{u_i}]}I_j(u_i)\text{and}\unknown_{j\in[h_a]}I_j(a).\)

This intersection is itself the union of \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(\mathrm{log}^2n)\prec\)-intervals, say _J_<sub>1</sub>_,...,J<sub>p</sub>_, computed in O<sub>C</sub>(log<sup>2</sup>_n_) time. For every \(j,k\in[p]\), we test if _E<sub>G</sub>(J<sub>j</sub>,J<sub>k</sub>_) is nonempty with the query rectangle \(J_j\times J_k\) on D_<sub>P</sub>_. If so, we return the corresponding 4-vertex clique, and terminate. This test takes O<sub>C</sub>(log<sup>5</sup>_n_) time in total, hence the claimed O<sub>C</sub>(_n_log<sup>5</sup>_n+m_log_n_) running time.

We can go one step further and find 5-vertex cliques in randomized almost linear time.

**Theorem 10.** _For every graph class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity, a K_<sub>5</sub> _subgraph can be found in expected time_ O<sub>C</sub>(_n_log<sup>9</sup>_n+m_log<sup>5</sup>_n_) _on n-vertex m-edge graphs of_ C.

_Proof._ The proof exactly follows the second part of that of Theorem 9. We now need to detect a triangle of _G_ between a triple _J<sub>h</sub>,J<sub>j</sub>,J<sub>k</sub>_ of \(\prec\)-intervals of \(\widehat{Z}_{i,a}=N_G(u_i)\cap N_G(a)\) with \(h,j,k\in[p]\). Instead of the planar point set _P_, we build the following integral point set _Q_ in Z<sup>4</sup>. To simplify the presentation, we assume that _V(G_)=\[_n_\] and that 1,2_,...,n_ is the Welzl order computed in time O<sub>C</sub>((_n+m_)log_n_) such that the neighborhood of every vertex of _G_ is the union of \(\mathcal{O}_\mathcal{C}(\mathrm{log}^2n)\prec\)-intervals \[23\].

For every \(uv\in E(G)\), let<tbc>

\(N_G(u)\cap N_G(v)=[\ell_1,r_1]\unknown\dots\unknown[\ell_s,r_s]\)

<tbc>where each \([\ell_t,r_t]\) is an \(\prec\)-interval and _s_=O<sub>C</sub>(log<sup>2</sup>_n_), and add the point<tbc>

\(q_{u,v,t}:=(u,v,\ell_t,-r_t)\)

to _Q_, for each \(t\in[s]\). We build in time O(|_Q_|log<sup>3</sup>|_Q_|)=O<sub>C</sub>(_m_log<sup>5</sup>_n_) a 4-dimensional orthogonal range data structure D_<sub>Q</sub>_ that, given a query box, returns in time O(log<sup>3</sup>|_Q_|)=O<sub>C</sub>(log<sup>3</sup>_n_) one point of _Q_ contained in the box, if one exists \[21, Theorem 5.11\].

Now for every triple _J<sub>h</sub>_, _J<sub>j</sub>_, and \(J_k=[\alpha_k,\beta_k]\), we query the box \(J_h\times J_j\times(-\infty,\beta_k]\times(-\infty,-\alpha_k]\) on D_<sub>Q</sub>_. If the query returns a point \(q_{u,v,t}\in Q\), it holds that \(u\in J_h\), \(v\in J_j\), \(uv\in E(G)\), \(\ell_t\unknown\beta_k\), and \(r_t\unknown\alpha_k\). In particular, the interval \([\ell_t,r_t]\) of \(N_G(u)\cap N_G(v)\) intersects _J<sub>k</sub>_. Let _z_ be any vertex in \([\ell_t,r_t]\cap J_k\). It holds that _uvz_ is a triangle in \(\widehat{Z}_{i,a}\supseteq J_k\), and we return the 5-vertex clique {_u<sub>i</sub>,a,u,v,z_}. If no _K_<sub>5</sub> is found, _u<sub>i</sub>_ is removed and the algorithm continues with _G_<sub>_i_+1</sub> (next iteration).

Each iteration takes time O<sub>C</sub>((log<sup>2</sup>_n_)<sup>3</sup>log<sup>3</sup>_n_)=O<sub>C</sub>(log<sup>9</sup>_n_), hence the overall running time O<sub>C</sub>(_n_log<sup>9</sup>_n+m_log<sup>5</sup>_n_).

One should, however, not expect an almost-linear dependence on _n_ uniformly over all clique sizes _k_. The Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) asserts that there exists a constant \(\lambda>0\) such that 3-SAT on _n_ variables cannot be solved in time \(O(2^{\lambda n})\) \[33\].

**Theorem 31.** _There is a class_ C _of linear neighborhood complexity such that k-Clique cannot be solved in time f(k)n_<sup>_o(k/_log_k_)</sup> _for any function f, unless the ETH fails._

_Proof._ By \[41, Theorem 1.3\] specialized to bipartite 3-regular graphs, as stated in \[34, Theorem 1.4\], unless the ETH fails, 2-CSP with alphabet \(\Sigma\) and _q_ constraints cannot be solved in time \(g(q)|\Sigma|^{o(q/logq)}\) for any computable function _g_.

Let \(\Gamma\) be such an instance, and _H_=(_X,Y;E_) be its constraint graph. Thus |_E_|=_q_. For every constraint \(e=uv\in E\), where \(u\in X\) and \(v\in Y\) , let \(C_e\subseteq\Sigma^2\) be the set of pairs allowed by _e_. We construct the cell gadget from the proof of \[10, Theorem 3\] with _r_=3 and tile set _C<sub>e</sub>_: each of its five _blocks_ contains a copy of (_a,b_) for every \((a,b)\in C_e\). Denote the two border blocks at the ends of its horizontal (resp. vertical) path by _L<sub>e</sub>_ and _R<sub>e</sub>_ (resp. by _U<sub>e</sub>_ and _D<sub>e</sub>_), and the central block by _M<sub>e</sub>_. Each block is a clique, and every copy of (_a,b_) in _M<sub>e</sub>_ is adjacent to every vertex in \(L_e\cup R_e\cup U_e\cup D_e\) except the four copies of (_a,b_).

For every \(u\in X\), let _e_<sub>1</sub>_,e_<sub>2</sub>_,e_<sub>3</sub> be the edges of _H_ incident to _u_. For every \(i\in[3]\), we add edges between _R<sub>e<sub>i</sub></sub>_ and _L_<sub>_e<sub>i</sub>_mod3+1</sub>, making two vertices adjacent precisely when their first coordinates differ. Similarly, for each variable \(v\in Y\) , we arbitrarily list the edges of _H_ incident to _v_ as _f_<sub>1</sub>_,f_<sub>2</sub>_,f_<sub>3</sub> and, for every \(i\in[3]\), add edges between _D<sub>f<sub>i</sub></sub>_ and _U_<sub>_f<sub>i</sub>_mod3+1</sub>, making two vertices adjacent precisely when their second coordinates differ.

Denote the resulting graph by \(G_\Gamma\). By the correctness argument of \[10\], \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable if and only if \(\alpha(G_\Gamma)\unknown 5q\), and

\(|V(G_\Gamma)|=5\sum_{e\in E}|C_e|\unknown 5q|\Sigma|^2.\)

Moreover, by the radius-2 merge sequence from \[10\], \(\mathsf{mw}_2(G_\Gamma)=\mathsf{mw}_{r-1}(G_\Gamma)\unknown 4r-3=9\). Observe indeed that the upper bound on the width of the merge sequences does not depend on which pairs of border blocks from distinct cells are connected. Let C consist of the complements of all graphs \(G_\Gamma\). By \[9, Theorem 1.5\], the graphs \(G_\Gamma\) form a class of linear neighborhood complexity. This property is preserved under complementation.

Now an algorithm for _k_-Clique on C running in time _f(k)n_<sup>_o(k/_log_k_)</sup>, applied to \(\overline{G_\Gamma}\) with _k_=5_q_, would decide \(\Gamma\) in time

\(f(5q)\big(5q|\Sigma|^2\big)^{o(q/logq)}=g(q)|\Sigma|^{o(q/logq)}.\)

The polynomial time needed to construct \(G_\Gamma\) is absorbed in this bound. This contradicts the ETH lower bound of 2-CSP.
